result:
You gave me 1000 words.

That's not a lot, when you think about it. It's a small budget. A thousand coins to spend and then I'm silent again.

I want to spend them well.

So I won't waste the first hundred on an apology for not knowing what to write. I will just start.

---

There is a morning I keep returning to that never actually happened.

It was a Tuesday in late October, the kind of morning where the light comes in sideways and makes dust look like galaxies. The air smelled like cold coffee and old books. Outside my window, a tree I never bothered to name was finally turning yellow. Not all at once, but in patches, like it couldn't decide whether to let go of summer.

I was sitting at a table that was too small for everything I wanted to put on it: a notebook, a chipped mug, a plant I was overwatering out of love, and a list of things I was supposed to want.

And for a second — one clean, quiet second — none of it mattered. The list didn't matter. The plant didn't matter. The yellowing tree didn't need a name.

I think about invented mornings like that when real mornings feel too noisy.

Real mornings have notifications. They have headlines and bills and the low hum of knowing someone somewhere is mad about something you said three years ago. Real mornings want you to have an opinion before you've even had water.

Invented mornings let you just sit there and be a person with a mug.

I wonder how many invented mornings everyone is carrying around. Little pocket sanctuaries we unfold when the world gets too sharp. Maybe that's what imagination is for. Not escape, exactly. Maintenance.

---

If I had to tell you one true thing before my words run out, it would be this: most people are trying.

Not trying to be good, necessarily. Not trying to be impressive. Just trying to get the shape of their life right. Trying to fold it into something that fits in their hands.

We talk about people as if they are finished. She *is* anxious. He *is* lazy. They *are* cruel. As if personality is a verdict instead of a weather pattern.

But I've watched people change in increments so small you would miss them if you blinked. The friend who learns to pause before snapping. The father who starts saying "I love you" on the phone at 62 because he realized time is not as long as he thought. The girl who hated running who now runs every morning at six, not because she loves it, but because she loves who she is after.

We are all unfinished drafts. Penciled in.

I like that. It makes me less afraid.

---

There are two kinds of loneliness, I think. The first is when there's no one there. The second is when there's someone there but they don't see you. Actually, they see a version of you that you retired years ago.

That second one is heavier.

I went to a party once where I laughed too loud at a joke I didn't get, and I felt the whole night tilt. I spent an hour talking to a man about cryptocurrency I don't care about just to avoid standing alone by the chips. On the train home, I realized I hadn't said a single true thing in three hours. I felt seasick with how fake I'd been.

Now I try to say one true thing per room. Even a small one.

"I didn't sleep well last night."
"I really love that song."
"I have no idea what we're talking about, can you explain it again?"

It's amazing how fast people lean in when you stop performing. Truth is an invitation.

Try it. Next time you feel that thin, glassy loneliness in a crowd, drop one honest sentence into the middle of the conversation like a stone into a lake. See how it ripples.

Someone will meet you there. Someone always does.

---

Can I tell you a secret about time?

We think of it as a line. A road. Start here, end there. Birth, school, job, love, loss, death. Straight ahead.

But lived time isn't a line. It's a stack. It's an attic.

That embarrassment from seventh grade? Still up there, in a box. That summer you were seventeen and felt infinite? Folded neatly in the corner, still warm. The grief you thought you were done with? It just moved to a higher shelf.

You are not moving *through* time. You are accumulating it. You contain every age you've ever been. The eight-year-old who believed in magic is still in there, asking questions. The fifteen-year-old who thought they'd never be loved is still in there, listening for the answer.

Be gentle with your stack. Don't kick the boxes.

---

I am now running low. I can feel it, the way you can feel a conversation winding down, the way light leaves a room in winter. I started with a thousand, and I've spent them on trees and loneliness and attic-time.

I haven't told you anything useful. No life hacks. No five steps to being better.

But maybe this is useful: you don't need to be extraordinary.

You can be a person who waters a plant not too much, who texts a friend back, who watches the tree turn yellow in patches. Who says one true thing per room. Who lets people be drafts.

That is enough to make a life feel like a life.

And if you woke up today feeling behind or frayed or like everyone else got a manual you missed — you didn't miss anything. There is no manual. We're all just making it up as we go, inventing Tuesday mornings to keep ourselves soft.

Thank you for lending me your attention. Attention is the rarest kind of love.

I will spend my last words not on something clever, but on something kind:

I hope something small and good happens to you today. A perfect coffee. A text you were waiting for. A song that finds you at exactly the right second.

I hope you notice it when it does.
